sections.title: Kiddushei Biah: U've'alah or a Kal Va'chomer from the Yevamah?
sections.gist: Continuing the baraita's sources for the modes of betrothal: why betrothal through intercourse needs the verse *u've'alah* and cannot rest on a *kal va'chomer* from the *yevamah*.

children.title: Yevamah and Amah Ivriyah: Proof, Counterproof, Rebuttal
children.gist: The *kal va'chomer* from the *yevamah* meets the *amah ivriyah* as a counterproof, which is set aside because her acquisition is not for marriage.

bullets.text: Baraita: “And engages in sexual intercourse with her” (*u've'alah*, Devarim 24:1) teaches that a woman can be acquired through intercourse.

Why is a verse needed? A *kal va'chomer*: a *yevamah*, who cannot be acquired with money, is acquired through intercourse; surely this woman, who can be acquired with money, is acquired through intercourse too.
Counterproof: the *amah ivriyah* is acquired with money, yet not through intercourse.
Rebuttal: her acquisition is not for the sake of marriage, while this woman's is. So the inference seems to stand.
Three cases run through the whole sugya: *yibbum*, the *amah ivriyah* and ordinary marriage. Deciding which comparisons are primary goes to the question of what *kiddushin* actually is.

Tosafot complicates the claim that the *amah ivriyah* is not acquired for marriage: the master may designate her (*ye'ud*) for himself or his son, and the purchase money then serves as betrothal money.

children.title: Rav Ashi: The Yevamah Is Already Bound, So the Verse Is Needed
children.gist: Rav Ashi breaks the *kal va'chomer* at its source: the *yevamah* is already bound to the *yavam*, which an ordinary woman is not.

bullets.text: The Gemara asks again: why the verse, if the *kal va'chomer* works?
Rav Ashi: the refutation is there from the outset. A *yevamah* is bound to the *yavam* and stands waiting for him, so intercourse suffices to make her his wife. An ordinary woman is bound to no one.
The inference does not survive scrutiny, so the verse *u've'alah* is required.

In the background is the tanna'im's dispute whether there is *zikah* and how strong it is. On some views, including R. Akiva's, it is close to betrothal, so *yibbum* completes a quasi-betrothed state.
Later dafim will ask whether intercourse effects only betrothal or full marriage (*nissuin*) at once.

sections.title: Kiddushei Shtar: Kal Va'chomer, Hekesh, and Excluding Divorce by Money
sections.gist: How a document betroths: a failed *kal va'chomer* from money, the *hekesh havayah le'yetziah* and why it doesn't run backward, and the verses that exclude divorce by money for Rava and for R. Yosei HaGelili.

children.title: Kal Va'chomer from Money, Refuted: Money Redeems Hekdesh
children.gist: If money, which cannot divorce, betroths, a document, which can, should betroth; but money has a unique power to redeem *hekdesh* and *ma'aser sheni*.

bullets.text: Baraita: money does not release a woman from her husband yet brings her into his domain; a document releases her (as a *get*), so surely it can bring her in.
Refutation: money redeems *hekdesh* and *ma'aser sheni*; a document cannot. Source for *hekdesh*: “And he will give the money and it will be assured to him” (see Vayikra 27:19).
The Mishnah lists money, document, intercourse, but the Gemara treats the document last. The pattern: try a *kal va'chomer* first, and spend a verse only when it fails.
Rashba: the power to permit is far greater than the power to forbid. A *get* permits a married woman to remarry, so the argument from its power is serious even though it fails.
What document would redeem *ma'aser sheni*? Rashi: a debt document. Rashba objects that betrothal and divorce documents are acquisition documents, like “these produce are redeemed by this document.”

children.title: Ve'yatzah Ve'hayetah: Documents Are Distinct, but the Coin Is One
children.gist: The verse compares entering marriage to leaving it, so a document betroths; the reverse comparison fails because one medium may not both bind and release, and only documents can be told apart.

bullets.text: “And she leaves his house… and becomes another man's wife” (Devarim 24:2) juxtaposes becoming (betrothal) with leaving (divorce): just as leaving is by document, becoming can be by document. This is the *hekesh havayah le'yetziah*.
Challenge: compare the other way. Just as becoming is by money, leaving should be by money.
Abaye: people would say “money brings in and money releases.” Can an advocate become a prosecutor?
Challenge: then say the same of a document. It brings in and releases; can a prosecutor become an advocate?

Answer: the words of a betrothal document and of a bill of divorce are distinct. Challenge: this coin and that coin are distinct too. Answer: the coin itself is one; nothing marks one coin for betrothal and another for divorce.

The principle *ein kateigor na'aseh saneigor* also rules out a cow's horn as a shofar and the Kohen Gadol's gold garments in the Holy of Holies. Money was the method actually used in Chazal's day, so the confusion was real.
Ba'al HaIttur: land cannot serve as betrothal money, since the *hekesh* imports the restrictions on a *get*. Rashba: the *hekesh* governs the document only, so land may serve as money.

Whether a *hekesh* inside a verse counts as a Torah-law source bears on the Rambam's shifting view of whether all three modes are Torah law; the final view, reported by R. Avraham ben HaRambam, is that all three are.

children.title: Rava: Ve'khatav Lah Excludes Divorce by Money, Not Betrothal by Document
children.gist: Rava reads “and he writes her” as excluding divorce by money, and the Gemara explains why that verse cannot instead exclude betrothal by document.

bullets.text: Rava: “And he writes her a scroll of severance” (Devarim 24:3): she is divorced only through writing, not through money.
Challenge: read it as “divorced through writing, but not betrothed through writing.” Answer: “and she leaves… and becomes” juxtaposes betrothal to divorce, so a document betroths.
Why not the reverse: the juxtaposition teaches money for both, and “he writes” excludes betrothal by writing? Because a verse speaking of divorce excludes a mode of divorce, not a mode of betrothal.

children.title: R. Yosei HaGelili and the Rabbis: Sefer Keritut and Complete Severance
children.gist: R. Yosei HaGelili learns from “a scroll severs” that money does not divorce; the Rabbis use *keritut* to require a *get* that severs completely, which R. Yosei derives from the form *keritut* rather than *karet*.

bullets.text: R. Yosei HaGelili uses “and he writes her” for another exposition. He learns from *sefer keritut* that a scroll severs her and nothing else does.
The Rabbis use *sefer keritut* for another rule: the *get* must entirely sever him from her.

Baraita (Tosefta Gittin 5:12): “Here is your *get* on condition you never drink wine” or “never go to your father's house” is not severance, since he restricts her forever; for thirty days, it is severance.
R. Yosei HaGelili derives complete severance from the verse's use of *keritut* rather than the basic *karet*. The Rabbis do not expound that difference.
A Rashba responsum and Tosafot take up the boundary cases: a condition for fifty years, or one that lasts until one of them dies.

sections.title: One from Two? Benefit, Wide Acquisition, or Against Her Will
sections.gist: No mode can be derived even from the other two: money and intercourse give great benefit, money and a document acquire widely, and intercourse and a document work against her will.

bullets.text: No mode comes from another single mode; why not derive one from the other two together?
A document from intercourse and money? Their benefit is great; a woman gets no enjoyment from receiving a document.
Intercourse from money and a document? Their acquisition is great: they acquire in many other situations, while intercourse is an unusual acquisition.
Money from intercourse and a document? They work against her will: a *yavam* acquires a *yevamah* even against her will, and a *get* releases a woman without her consent.
Suggestion: money also works against her will, for the *amah ivriyah* whom her father sells. Rejected: in marriage, money never acquires a woman against her will.

Sha'ar HaMelekh: if intercourse works through its pleasure, what of intercourse with less pleasure? Perhaps what counts is the act of acquisition itself, and “great benefit” describes the category rather than the mechanism.
Tosafot (3a) considers and rejects comparing intercourse to *chazakah*, the physical act that acquires land.

sections.title: Rav Huna: Does Chuppah Betroth by Kal Va'chomer?
sections.gist: Rav Huna's argument that *chuppah* alone betroths, in two versions (it permits *terumah*; it completes the marriage), the *tzad ha'shaveh* cycle that defends it, and Rava's two refutations with Abaye's replies.

children.title: First Version: Chuppah Permits Terumah, Undone by Ulla
children.gist: Rav Huna argues from *terumah*, but Ulla shows that by Torah law betrothal money already lets her eat *terumah*.

bullets.text: Rav Huna: *chuppah* acquires by *kal va'chomer*. Money does not let a betrothed Israelite woman eat her *kohen* husband's *terumah*, yet it acquires her; *chuppah*, which lets her eat it, should surely acquire her.

Challenge from Ulla: by Torah law a betrothed Israelite woman may eat *terumah* at once: “if a *kohen* buy any soul, the acquisition of his money, he may eat of it” (Vayikra 22:11), and she is his *kinyan kaspo*.

She is kept from it only by rabbinic decree, lest they pour her a cup of *terumah* wine in her father's house and she share it with her brothers and sisters, for whom it is forbidden. The premise falls.
The rishonim hold some seven views of what *chuppah* is: a shared garment, a canopy, veiling the bride, seclusion, intercourse, or entering his home. Each has legal consequences.

children.title: Second Version: Chuppah Completes the Marriage; the Tzad Ha'shaveh Cycle
children.gist: Recast: money, which does not complete the marriage, betroths, so *chuppah*, which does, should betroth too. The Gemara tests this against each mode, and Rav Huna's *tzad ha'shaveh* survives.

chart.caption: The features the Gemara weighs in testing *chuppah* against the three modes (5a–5b)
rows: Only for the *amah ivriyah*, never in marriage
No: only if she enters willingly

children.title: Money and Intercourse: Their Common Denominator
children.gist: Money's special power is answered by intercourse, intercourse's by money, and what the two share, that they acquire generally, is found in *chuppah* too.

bullets.text: The Gemara recasts Rav Huna: money does not complete the acquisition, since a *na'arah* stays under her father's authority in some matters, yet it betroths. *Chuppah* removes her from his authority entirely, so it should betroth on its own.
Objection: money redeems *hekdesh* and *ma'aser sheni*; *chuppah* acquires nothing but a wife.
Intercourse proves otherwise: it acquires a woman though it acquires nothing else.
Intercourse is unique: it acquires a *yevamah*, and a *yavam* does not acquire her by *chuppah*. Money proves otherwise: it does not acquire a *yevamah*, yet acquires a woman.
*Tzad ha'shaveh*: the two are not alike, but both acquire generally and acquire here. *Chuppah* also acquires generally (it makes her a married woman), so it should acquire here.

children.title: Great Benefit? The Document Answers
children.gist: The objection that money and intercourse give great benefit is answered by the document, and the document's power to divorce by money and intercourse.

bullets.text: Objection: the common denominator of money and intercourse is their great pleasure. The document proves otherwise: no great pleasure, yet it acquires.
The document is unique: it releases a woman as a *get*. Money and intercourse prove otherwise: they do not release, yet they acquire.
The argument returns to its *tzad ha'shaveh*: all acquire generally and acquire here, so *chuppah* should too.

children.title: Against Her Will: Rav Huna's Answer from Marriage
children.gist: All three modes work against her will somewhere and *chuppah* does not; Rav Huna answers that in marriage money never does, so the derivation stands.

bullets.text: Objection: all three work against her will in some case: a *get*, intercourse with a *yevamah*, money for the *amah ivriyah*. *Chuppah* works only when she enters it willingly.
Rav Huna: in marriage, money never acquires a woman against her will. So the three modes do show that *chuppah* betroths.

returns_to.note: The same point about money and the *amah ivriyah* that blocked deriving money from the other two

children.title: Rava's Two Refutations, Abaye's Two Replies
children.gist: Rava: the Mishnah counts three modes, and *chuppah* completes a marriage only after betrothal. Abaye: the Mishnah lists only what is written, and Rav Huna's argument already builds on the second point.

bullets.text: Rava's first refutation: the Mishnah teaches three modes, not four.
Rava's second: *chuppah* completes a marriage only by means of the betrothal before it. One cannot learn *chuppah* without betrothal from *chuppah* that works through betrothal.
Abaye: the *tanna* lists only what is explicit in the Torah, and *chuppah* is not.

Abaye: that is Rav Huna's very point. Money after money does not complete the marriage (a second gift does not make her fully married), yet money betroths; *chuppah* completes after money, so it is stronger and should betroth by itself.
Tosafot HaRosh: does Rav Huna mean that *chuppah* betroths and completes the marriage at once, or betroths only? The sugya leaves it open.
The halakha usually follows Rava over Abaye, but the Rif may rule like Rav Huna. A practical case is rare, such as a bride who dies after the veiling, before any conventional betrothal.

children.title: He Gives and Says: Betrothed; She Gives and Says: Not
children.gist: The baraita sets out the man's giving with a formula of betrothal as valid, and the woman's giving with her own formula as invalid.

bullets.text: Baraita (Tosefta 1:1): he gave money or its worth and said “You are hereby betrothed (*mekudeshet*) to me,” “betrothed (*me'oreset*) to me” or “to me as a wife”: she is betrothed.
If she gave him the money and said “I am hereby betrothed to you” (or the like): she is not betrothed.
This follows “when a man takes a woman”: the man is the active party.

children.title: Rav Pappa: He Gives, She Says? Not Betrothed or Uncertain
children.gist: Rav Pappa finds the baraita's two clauses implying opposite rulings for the mixed case; after a retracted answer, the Gemara reads it either as not betrothed or as uncertain.

bullets.text: Rav Pappa: the first clause implies that if he gave and she spoke, she is not betrothed; the last clause implies that she is.
Answer: the first clause is exact, and the last was worded only to mirror it. Challenge: would the baraita teach a clause that contradicts the first? The answer is retracted.
First explanation: if he gave and she spoke, it is as though she gave and spoke, so she is not betrothed.
Second explanation: if he gave and she spoke, it is uncertain, and by rabbinic law we are concerned it may be a betrothal.
The verbal formula appears nowhere in the verse, yet her saying it can undo his valid giving. What the formula accomplishes is the question Shmuel's rule takes up next.

sections.title: Shmuel: The Formula Must Change Her Status, Not His
sections.gist: Shmuel: formulas about her betrothal or divorce work and formulas about himself (“I am your husband”) raise no concern. Rav Pappa asks whether this means ambiguous intimations count; the Gemara answers that Shmuel's case says “to me.”
sections.continues: Continues on 6a: a baraita's two sets of three betrothal formulas, and questions about further expressions such as “designated to me” and “my taken one.”

children.title: “You Are Betrothed” vs. “I Am Your Husband,” and the Same in Divorce
children.gist: In betrothal and in divorce alike, a formula about the woman takes effect, and one about the man raises no concern at all.

bullets.text: Shmuel: he gave money or its worth and said “You are hereby betrothed (*mekudeshet*),” “betrothed (*me'oreset*)” or “as a wife”: she is betrothed.
If he said “I am hereby your man,” “your husband” or “your betrothed”: there is no room for concern.

Divorce: he gave a *get* and said “You are hereby sent away,” “divorced” or “permitted to any man”: she is divorced. “I am not your man,” “not your husband” or “not your betrothed”: no room for concern.
Betrothal does not change the man's status: he may still marry another wife. It is she who becomes forbidden to other men and needs a *get*, so a formula about him says nothing.

children.title: Yadayim She'einan Mochiot? Rav Pappa's Nazirite Challenge
children.gist: Rav Pappa asks whether Shmuel's “you are betrothed” without “to me” means ambiguous intimations count, contrary to Shmuel on the nazirite; the Gemara answers that the case says “to me,” and Shmuel's point is the formulas about the man.

bullets.text: Rav Pappa to Abaye: “You are hereby betrothed” lacks “to me.” Does Shmuel hold that *yadayim she'einan mochiot* (ambiguous intimations) count?

But on the Mishnah (Nazir 2a) that one who says “I shall be” is a nazirite, Shmuel said: only when a nazirite was passing before him; otherwise he might mean a fast. So ambiguous intimations do not count.
Answer: Shmuel speaks of one who did say “to me.” What is new, then? The last expressions: “I am your husband” raises no concern at all.
Why: “When a man takes a woman” (Devarim 24:1): he takes her, not himself. And “and sends her”: he sends her, not himself.

key_terms.definition: An argument from a lesser case to a greater one: if a rule holds where there is less reason for it, it holds all the more where there is more reason. It fails if the lesser case has some feature the greater lacks.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara tries to derive intercourse, a document and chuppah as modes of betrothal by kal va'chomer, and refutes each attempt except Rav Huna's, which Rava challenges.

key_terms.sense: the bond between yavam and yevamah
key_terms.definition: The legal bond that links a childless man's widow to his surviving brother from the moment of his death, until yibbum or chalitzah.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Ashi: because a yevamah is already bound to the yavam, her acquisition through intercourse proves nothing for an ordinary woman.

key_terms.sense: juxtaposing entry into marriage with its dissolution
key_terms.definition: The comparison, drawn from Devarim 24:2, between how a woman becomes married and how she leaves a marriage, so that the modes of the one inform the other.
key_terms.on_this_daf: It teaches that a document betroths as a get divorces; the Gemara explains why it does not also make money divorce.

key_terms.sense: a prosecutor cannot become an advocate
key_terms.definition: The principle that the same thing should not serve opposite roles, such as an instrument of accusation serving for defense, or a means of binding serving for release.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Abaye uses it to explain why money, which betroths, cannot also divorce, while distinct documents can serve for both.

key_terms.definition: A derivation from two or more sources that differ from one another: what they share is the ground for applying their rule to a new case. It fails if the sources share another feature the new case lacks.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Huna's case for chuppah rests on the tzad ha'shaveh of money, intercourse and the document, which survives the objections of benefit, divorce and consent.

key_terms.definition: The second stage of marriage, following betrothal, which brings the woman fully into her husband's domain; its exact form is debated.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Huna argues that chuppah alone can betroth; Rava objects that chuppah completes a marriage only after betrothal.

key_terms.definition: The requirement that a bill of divorce cut the tie between husband and wife entirely, so that he keeps no lasting hold over her.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Yosei HaGelili learns from sefer keritut that only a document divorces; the Rabbis learn that a get with a permanent condition is not severance.

key_terms.definition: An incomplete formula (a "handle") whose meaning is clear only from context. Whether such a statement takes legal effect is debated.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Pappa asks whether Shmuel's "you are hereby betrothed" without "to me" shows that Shmuel accepts them; the Gemara says Shmuel's case includes "to me."

judgment_calls: Rava's derivation from ve'khatav lah (s7) and R. Yosei HaGelili's sefer keritut (s8) are kept under the document section, since they arise from the question of why money does not divorce; they could instead form their own top-level section on divorce by money.
The 'one from two' discussion (s9) is a top-level section, since it caps all three modes; it could have been a child of the document section, where it falls.
The tzad ha'shaveh cycle in Rav Huna's second version is split into three children by objection (money/intercourse, benefit, against her will); it could have been one section with a long bullet list.
Rava's refutations and Abaye's replies (s16) stay under Rav Huna rather than standing alone, since they test his argument.
The baraita on giving and saying (s17) and Shmuel's formulas (s20) are two top-level sections; they could be one section on the mechanics of betrothal by money.
s15 is linked back to s9 with returns_to, since it reuses the point about money and the amah ivriyah.
coverage_notes: The essay reverses two of the 'one from two' refutations: it says deriving money fails because intercourse and document are not 'normal' acquisitions, and deriving intercourse fails because intercourse cannot be against her will. The text: deriving intercourse fails because money and document have 'great acquisition,' and deriving money fails because intercourse (yevamah) and document (get) work against her will. Followed the text.

The essay says Rav Huna has no answer to the against-her-will objection and the kal va'chomer cannot be completed; the text says Rav Huna answers that in marriage money never acquires against her will, so the derivation stands. Followed the text.
The essay presents 'the first clause is exact' as the Gemara's resolution of Rav Pappa's question; the text retracts that answer and gives two other explanations. Followed the text.

The essay gives the nazirite case as saying 'aha'; the text has 'I shall be' (Mishnah Nazir 2a). The essay also omits the Gemara's answer that Shmuel's case is one where he said 'to me,' and that the novelty is the second set of expressions. Followed the text.

In the second version of Rav Huna's argument, the essay starts with intercourse as the counterproof; the text first refutes by money's power to redeem hekdesh and ma'aser sheni, and only then brings intercourse. Followed the text's order.

The essay describes the Tosafot on the amah ivriyah as saying the father's sale is not against her will; the text itself treats it as against her will and deflects it as not marriage. Left the Tosafot point out to avoid confusion with the text.

All lines 4b.10 through 6a.1 are discussed in the shiur; no section is flagged. The shiur's forward reference to the question whether intercourse effects betrothal or full marriage (later dafim) is noted only in passing.
